## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#one-number-thirty-people}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Everyone who chose the same analyst got **the same *t***, to the third decimal. That is reproducibility, and once the data and the code are in hand it is the easy R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Across the three analysts the *t* runs from −1.206 to −7.169, on one claim, under one set of instructions. Each analyst wrote their own code.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of them was careless. The numbers differ because the analysts made different choices about the data and the model.
:::
::::

::: notes
Look at what just happened. Everyone who chose the same analyst landed on the same number, to the third decimal, on different machines. That is reproducibility, and notice how cheap it was once the data and the code were in hand: you ran the same code on the same file, so of course you got the same number. [pause] Now look across the three groups in the chat. Minus one point two, minus three point eight, minus seven point two, for one claim, from analysts who were given the same instructions. Not one of them was careless. I have read the code of the other four line by line, and they are competent, well-organised pipelines written by people who knew what they were doing. The spread comes from choices about the data and the model, and choices of that kind are what robustness, the second R, is about.
:::
